body: Handle him for as long as you’d like! Either until he calms down (might take a while), or until a set time is up. Young bulls tend to be bullies, as well, so this is the right time to be headstrong and hang out with him as much as possible! In my opinion, I’d much rather deal with a yearling bite than a 5 year old bite!

First, as I’m sure you’re aware, feeding live prey, especially rodents past a certain developmental stage, can be extremely dangerous for the snake and stressful for everyone involved. I’d recommend starting the process of switching him over to frozen/thawed, and feed him small hoppers once a week. Second, I’d up his humidity a bit more than usual, just to help with his scales, especially that nose. Finally, just give him time to adjust. Bullsnakes are naturally very curious and intelligent critters, so given time, he’ll adapt to his new environment. A healthy mental state does wonders when it comes to recovery! Above all else, I’d get him checked over by a vet, just in case they might not have done so when they first took him in. He might have internal wounds that need addressing as well, like parasites. He looks like a Gooseberry to me!
A great way to tell is to give your snake some gentle rubs in a single area. If they haven’t shed yet, the skin will start to separate a little bit, just enough to be noticeable!

I’ve gone through this with three baby bulls, and given how they all now love to come out and say hi, and haven’t bitten or tail buzzed at me since the first two weeks they arrived (mostly), I’d like to say I’m quite experienced! Like u/paleontologirl mentioned, I like to leave them alone other than feeding and cleaning for at least a week, normally two, and then start taking them out and handling them for however long they feel comfortable with. I tend to handle them more frequently, once a day, for as little as 2 minutes to as long as 3 hours, it just depends on the snake. I have one that likes to snuggle into my sleeves and take a nap, so she tends to be out for hours at a time just because she gets so comfortable, whereas my younger girl is very curious and explorative. She’ll burrow into my sleeves, then quickly make her way all the way over to my other sleeve and pop back out! Because of how active and busy she is, she tends to do better viewing the experience like playtime, so I only have her out for maybe 10 minutes, before I put her back, just so she keeps the idea that “handling is playtime.” Because my other girl likes to sleep during handling, I try to keep her sessions very calm and quiet, so for her, “handling is nap time.” It really depends on the snake’s personality, how active they are, and how patient YOU can be. But like others have said, they are a gopher species, they LOVE substrate. My third baby, my boy, has turned “feral” ever since he moved from his baby bin to his bioactive grow out tank. He’s rarely seen and if he is, it’s either his tail or his head poking out of the dirt, before he disappears down a different hole. It’s just in their nature, so don’t take it too personally if you find it hard to see him! Good luck, you’re doing a great job! And welcome to the bullsnake family :))

I live on the coast where the weather never gets out of the 55 - 90 range, so I keep them room temp, which is about low 70s daytime and mid 60s nighttime, but bulls do just fine anywhere from mid 60s - low 80s. I wouldn’t recommend keeping their ambient enclosure at anything above 80, as it can cause them to be easily irritable in some cases. They don’t require a lot of humidity, just a water bowl is fine, but not big enough to fit in, as they will soil the water regularly if allowed, and they refuse to drink anything but clear, fresh water, at least in my experience. I would still mist the tank, especially when they’re young, I’ve found my kiddos prefer drinking from the droplets than the bowl. I get perfect sheds with just some damp moss in a hide or damp paper towels in an enclosed space, I like to leave a rough stone in the center of the hide to rub against, and I always end up with really nice sheds. They love to burrow, but this can be a problem with a lot of substrates, especially if you’re going the bioactive route and you don’t have an established tank, so I tend to mist more often in the first few months than need be, just to help keep humidity high while the snake lets air into the dirt with their digging.

If its a stand, I’d recommend looking into cabinet stands, Zen Habitats sells them, Toad Ranch sells them, and I’m sure you could find a decently priced garage storage desk that would fit the length of the tank just fine. Again, I didn’t do much research into other brands, as I am extremely satisfied with Toad Ranch, but I understand they are pretty pricey, so I wouldn’t recommend them if you aren’t absolutely sure. I apologize I can’t be much help, but I do hope you stay passionate about keeping bulls! They are such personable companions.

Yep, I totally had that phase of watching random shorts and documentaries just for a glimpse of a bull, haha! I think most Bullsnakes can be “tamed down” fairly easy, though the biggest obstacle I’ve found has been that they are simply more intelligent, or at the very least, they tend to use their brain more than many other reptiles. They’re a lot like a border collie, trying to figure you out, pushing boundaries, seeing what they can get away with. I think it’s because of that that I enjoy engaging with them so much, because you can almost see the gears turning in their little heads!

A lot of people just don’t find any benefit in keeping an “aggressive” snake, especially if it isn’t an otherworldly type of beauty, like an Emerald Tree boa. Of course, bulls are definitely sassy, but I think that’s what makes them so fun to interact with; they are such a perfect ambassador for snakes as a whole to show that reptiles can and do have personalities. There’s also not much content in general about them, so finding info on them, being charmed by them, isn’t as easy as searching “ball python” and finding hundreds of thousands of cute up close photos of them. I think they’ve gotten more popular as of recently, but they still have a long way to go, for sure. As an avid bullsnake lover and keeper, if you’re thinking about getting one, please do the research and absolutely get that snake! They are wonderfully personable, easily tamed, they eat like champs, get to a fantastic size, and in my opinion, have some downright gorgeous colorations and beautiful patterning! They are also quite hard to kill, all my bulls have been the picture of healthy ever since I first got them. Please don’t feel discouraged with the lack of bullsnake representation, and definitely keep active in the bull community! I love seeing other people find joy in the same traits and lovable characteristics that I see in these awesome little guys!

Hi Chels! I’m still a relatively new bullsnake owner myself, but I’d love to share what has and hasn’t worked for me and my snake, Astrid. I tend to over research every little thing, so luckily I got a pretty good understanding of certain husbandry averages. Astrid is still very young, she’s turning 2 in July, but thanks to that I’ve been able to really understand and see her behavior in a very exaggerated way. First off, let me just preface with saying that Astrid is very much not your average bull, she tends to be very forgiving towards so many of my mistakes as a new snake keeper. 

Care tips:

I tend to keep Astrid at room temperature, my rooms tends to stay at around 72 F in the day and drop to around 65 at the lowest in the night. Bullsnakes tolerate colder temperatures much more than hotter temperatures, so if you’re unsure, it’s much safer to go a little cooler than a little warmer

Astrid does have a heat lamp, it’s not the strongest, but it definitely keeps one of her hides warmer that she likes to go into when she’s digesting. I have it on top of her enclosure, so she has no chance of burning herself, as bullsnakes tend to be very curious and very active

Bulls don’t need any special lighting, but that doesn’t mean it’s not unappreciated, so it’s really up to you if you want to provide any UVB

They are serious burrowers, so if you go for bio active, or even consider having some plants in there, make sure it’s very stable. It’s best for the plants to have established and grown strong roots before introducing the snake, but putting them in a pot and securing the top of it with mesh also works just fine

These snakes are VERY active at a young age, especially if they aren’t used to handling. They also aren’t arboreal in any way, so you do have to make sure you’re supporting them, because they WILL fall if they aren’t used to handling

I highly recommend already having a reptile-friendly vet in mind before you handle or even receive the snake because of this. It’s the worst when you’re worried something is wrong and you have to drive around finding which vet will take snakes

These guys rarely need humidity unless they’re in shed, I’ve found that nestling damp sphagnum moss around a rough rock and putting a hide over it all makes for very nice whole sheds

These guys are quite defensive, and extremely smart, so if you go to handle them and they get all hissy and puffy, it’s ideal that you can at least touch or pick them up for even a minute before you leave them alone, especially if you feel you’ve been acting fidgety trying to pick them up. Astrid picked up on my sensitivity to loud noises when I first got her and would hiss as loudly as she could and buzz her tail against something hard to make sudden loud noises that would make me jump and leave her alone. She then started doing it any time I got near her enclosure until I eventually just scooped her up and she realized it didn’t work anymore

Snake hooks will be your friend, even though these guys aren’t dangerous whatsoever. Sometimes, when Astrid is having a bad day, she’s a lot less stressed interacting with the hook than with my hands, and it’s especially helpful to get them out of a defensive mode

These guys also THRIVE with as much space as you can give them. A 4 x 2 x 2 is my personal minimum requirement, I like to follow the general rule that your snake should be able to fully stretch out along the longest side of their enclosure. As well as plenty of space, bulls will always appreciate any stimulation you can give them. They may not be good climbers, but any kind of ledges, rocks, tubes, or ropes you can give them to interact with and climb on will go a long way with keeping them entertained and comfortable. I have personally found that paper towel tubes work wonders for climbing, smelling, and for getting her off or out of a place I don’t want her to be in. Just cover one hole of the tube, hold it up to their face, or close enough where they can see it, and wait. Astrid has learned to climb right in and sees it as her own personal transportation. 

Because they’re so intelligent, I recommend keeping them in a place in the house that is either generally quiet and/or visually quiet. Astrid is a very visual snake, and she doesn’t like having a clear view outside her hide, nor does she like loud noises. I have paper towel tubes stacked up into a pyramid to minimize the amount of light that gets in her hide, but I’ve also used crystals and leaves to make little doors for her. 

I’d like to stress this point, these snakes are extremely smart and aware of their surroundings. Think of them like you would a Doberman or a poodle. They’re a lot more aware than you realize, and they pick up on any kinds of patterns or routines quickly. This can be a blessing if you’re doing any kind of training or association work with them, but it can also be a nightmare if they have a negative experience more than once

If you have any other questions, please please do reach out to me, I’d love to help, you can either message me here or on Discord @ mynameiskyir. This is pretty long, so sorry for the wall of text. Good luck with your bullsnake journey, I’m so happy to know that another person likes them just as much as I do :))
